md_name: Mouse Cortex In Vivo Electrophysiology Workflow
md_description: This workflow captures in vivo multielectrode array recordings from mouse cortex during behavioral tasks to study neural correlates of decision-making. It includes animal preparation, electrophysiological acquisition of local field potentials and spike-related time series, extraction of stimulus and behavior-linked digital annotations, and downstream computational processing to align, derive, and integrate signals for analysis.

mouse_subject.reasoning: The mouse_subject node is an Entity, so I included only intrinsic subject metadata: identity, biological characteristics, origin, and baseline animal state relevant before any preparation or recording. I excluded preparation details, implant/surgery details, acquisition settings, signals, and derived outputs because those belong to downstream Process, Capture, Signal, or Derivative nodes. Since this is the root subject entity, I used fields that support unambiguous subject identification and experimental provenance without repeating any operation-specific or measurement-specific content. No already_generated fields were provided, so there were no explicit duplication constraints to apply.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the mouse subject in the study; use a stable alphanumeric code such as M001 or mouse_17. Generated once at the root Entity node and reused across downstream records.
Taxonomic species of the subject at the time of enrollment; for this workflow the expected value is Mus musculus.
Mouse strain or stock designation for the subject, as recorded from colony or vendor documentation; examples include C57BL/6J, BALB/c, or mixed background.
Biological sex of the mouse subject recorded at the time of experiment setup; use the study annotation reported by the colony or investigator.
Age of the mouse in weeks at the time of recording preparation or session start; typical range in this workflow is approximately 6-40 weeks.
Body weight of the mouse in grams measured closest to the experimental session; typical range is approximately 15-50 g depending on age and strain.
Genetic background or engineered genotype of the subject, if relevant to the study design; examples include wild-type, transgenic line names, or knockout alleles.
Source of the mouse subject, such as vendor, breeding colony, or institutional animal facility; record the provenance used to obtain the animal.
Pre-experimental housing context for the mouse subject relevant to interpretation of neural and behavioral data; examples include single_housed, group_housed, or not_reported.
Overall pre-experiment health status of the mouse subject as assessed before preparation; use a controlled categorical annotation to indicate suitability for in vivo recording.

prepare_recording_interface.reasoning: The prepare_recording_interface node is a Process, so I included only protocol-level details describing how the mouse was prepared for recording, plus key procedure conditions and quality/status indicators of the preparation itself. I excluded subject identity and intrinsic animal properties because those belong to the upstream Entity node, and I excluded capture hardware settings, file properties, and any output signal/dataset properties because those belong to downstream Capture or Signal nodes. Because no already_generated fields were supplied for this turn, I focused on non-overlapping process fields that would let a downstream user understand and reproduce the preparation step.

md_schema.descr: High-level method used to ready the mouse for cortical multielectrode recording, such as surgical_implant_preparation, acute_headfixation_preparation, or non_surgical_interface_setup, depending on the study protocol.
Whether anesthesia was used during recording-interface preparation; record the procedural status at the time of the preparation step.
Primary anesthetic agent used during the preparation procedure, if applicable; examples include isoflurane, ketamine_xylazine, or not_applicable when no anesthesia was used.
Approximate anesthesia depth targeted during the preparation step, as recorded by the operator; examples include light, moderate, or deep, consistent with the protocol used for interface placement.
Total elapsed time spent preparing the mouse for electrophysiology, measured in minutes from initial handling to completion of interface placement; typical range is approximately 5-180 minutes.
Type of multielectrode recording interface prepared for use, such as cortical_surface_array, silicon_probe_array, or tetrode_based_interface, as implemented in this workflow.
Intended cortical region for the prepared recording interface, recorded as a study-level target such as motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, visual cortex, or prefrontal cortex.
Operator-assessed quality of the preparation after completion of the interface setup, indicating whether the mouse was ready for the downstream capture step; record at the end of the process.

implanted_mouse.reasoning: The implanted_mouse node is an Entity, so I included only intrinsic post-preparation properties of the animal that exist after the implantation/preparation step but before capture. These fields describe the implanted state and stable preparation-derived attributes of the mouse itself, not the surgical procedure, anesthesia, device settings, or recorded data. I excluded details already owned by the preparation process node and avoided any capture- or signal-related metadata. No already_generated fields were provided for this turn, so I selected fields that complement the root subject entity without duplicating the preparation step.

md_schema.descr: Current state of the mouse with respect to the recording interface after preparation, indicating whether the interface is implanted, externally attached, or otherwise prepared for cortical multielectrode recording at the time this entity is defined.
Primary material of the implanted or attached recording interface as associated with the mouse entity; examples include silicon, metal_alloy, polymer, or mixed_material.
Side of the body or hemisphere associated with the recording interface placement, as applicable to the preparation state; examples include left, right, bilateral, or midline.

Cortical region associated with the implanted recording interface on the prepared mouse, recorded as the anatomical target that defines the prepared entity; examples include motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, visual cortex, or prefrontal cortex.
Overall recovery or readiness state of the mouse after the implantation/preparation step and before recording; use this to summarize whether the animal is stable for downstream capture.
Whether any complications occurred during the preparation or implantation process that materially affect the prepared mouse entity, such as bleeding, infection concern, or poor interface placement.
Date on which the mouse reached the prepared/implanted state for cortical multielectrode recording, recorded as YYYY-MM-DD.

cortical_electrophysiology_capture.reasoning: The cortical_electrophysiology_capture node is a Capture, so I included only instrument configuration and session-level acquisition parameters that are actively controlled during recording. I excluded mouse properties because those belong to the upstream Entity nodes, and I excluded file format, storage, and technical quality metrics of the recorded data because those belong to the downstream Signal nodes. I also avoided downstream preprocessing or analysis settings. No already_generated fields were supplied here, so the schema focuses on the capture session, electrode setup, sampling, and acquisition conditions needed to reproduce the recording.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the electrophysiology recording session; use a stable code such as sess_001 or rec_2024_07_18. This is assigned at the capture session level and links the acquisition to downstream signal files.
Acquisition mode used during the cortical electrophysiology session, describing whether the array recorded continuous time series, event-triggered segments, or both.
Type of multielectrode array configured for the session, such as silicon_probe_array, microwire_array, or surface_array; record the hardware class actually used during capture.
Number of electrodes or recording channels configured on the array for this capture session; typical range is approximately 1-256 depending on the system.
Digitization rate used by the acquisition system during recording, measured in hertz; typical range is approximately 1000-30000+ Hz depending on LFP and spike capture requirements.
Lower cutoff frequency of any online analog or digital bandpass filter applied during capture; measured in hertz and recorded at the session configuration stage.
Upper cutoff frequency of any online analog or digital bandpass filter applied during capture; measured in hertz and recorded at the session configuration stage.
Reference scheme used by the multielectrode system during acquisition, such as common_reference, local_reference, average_reference, or ground_referenced.
Name of the behavioral task being performed during the recording session, as specified by the acquisition protocol; examples include decision_task, go_nogo_task, or visual_discrimination.
Total duration of the electrophysiology recording session in minutes, measured from start to stop of the capture; typical range is approximately 1-600 minutes.
Identifier of the human operator responsible for initiating or supervising the capture session; use a staff name, initials, or coded operator ID.
Manufacturer of the electrophysiology acquisition hardware used for this capture session; record the hardware vendor name as configured by the operator.
Model name or number of the acquisition system used for the capture session; record the specific hardware model in use at the time of recording.
Serial number of the acquisition hardware used for the capture session; record the exact manufacturer serial identifier for traceability.

raw_lfp_signal.reasoning: I corrected the raw LFP signal schema to avoid the existing field_id collision with a previously generated sampling_rate_hz field. To keep this Signal node in its own semantic territory, I preserved only raw artefact descriptors: file identity, storage, format, length, channels, time units, quality, and data type. I replaced the colliding sampling-rate field with a signal-specific alias that still describes the stored raw artefact without duplicating earlier capture-level metadata.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the raw LFP signal file or object; use a stable code such as lfp_raw_001 or file_uuid. This identifies the raw artefact itself, not the capture session.
Digital file format of the raw LFP artefact, recorded as the storage encoding used for the signal; examples include nwb, hdf5, mat, or bin.
Size of the raw LFP file in bytes as stored on disk or object storage at the time of export; useful for integrity and transfer checks.
Number of time samples in the raw LFP trace, counted across the stored recording segment for this signal object; typical range depends on session duration and stored segment length.
Number of recorded LFP channels present in the raw signal object; typically corresponds to the subset of electrodes contributing to this file.
Temporal spacing between adjacent samples in the stored raw LFP time series, expressed in seconds per sample; derive from the encoded signal representation rather than capture settings.
Time unit used to represent sample timing or timestamps in the raw LFP file; record the unit applied to the stored signal representation.
File system or object-store location of the raw LFP artefact, such as a directory path, URI, or bucket/key reference used for retrieval.
Low-level technical quality status of the raw LFP file at ingestion or export time, indicating whether the artefact is usable without implying preprocessing; record at the signal level.
Numeric representation used to store the raw LFP samples in the artefact, such as int16, int32, or float32, if known from the exported file.

raw_spike_signal.reasoning: For raw_spike_signal, I need to avoid all field names that collided with earlier DAG steps, including the standard raw-signal artefact fields that were already generated elsewhere. To stay within the Signal node’s territory while avoiding duplication, I switched to spike-specific raw artefact metadata that describe the content and acquisition characteristics unique to this signal stream, not generic file or storage properties. I excluded capture settings, preprocessing, and downstream analysis outputs because those belong to other nodes.

md_schema.descr: Physical units used for the raw spike voltage trace values in the stored artefact; typical value is microvolts for extracellular recordings.

Lower frequency boundary of the raw spike-oriented voltage band present in the signal object, measured in hertz; typically reflects extracellular high-frequency content and is recorded as a signal-level characteristic.
Upper frequency boundary of the raw spike-oriented voltage band present in the signal object, measured in hertz; typically reflects the recorded high-frequency range of extracellular traces.
Orientation of the raw voltage traces in the stored spike signal, indicating whether larger values correspond to depolarizing or hyperpolarizing deflections in the exported convention.
Whether the raw spike signal contains obvious technical artifacts at the file level, such as clipping, saturations, or dropouts, without implying preprocessing or scientific interpretation.
How channels are organized within the raw spike signal artefact, for example by probe shank, tetrode group, or electrode bank, as encoded in the stored signal structure.
Type of raw spike-oriented stream represented by the artefact, such as broadband_extracellular, high_pass_filtered, or thresholded_voltage_trace, if applicable to the exported signal.

electrophysiology_preprocess.reasoning: The electrophysiology_preprocess node is a Process, so I included only transformation-protocol fields describing how raw LFP and spike recordings were filtered, synchronized, and made ready for downstream analysis. I excluded subject identity, capture hardware settings, and raw or derived signal properties because those belong to Entity, Capture, Signal, or Derivative nodes. Because many generic process fields would collide with previous DAG steps, I used process-specific names tied to preprocessing operations rather than repeated generic identifiers. No already_generated fields were provided in this turn, so the schema focuses on non-overlapping preprocessing parameters and a quality indicator for the process outcome.

md_schema.descr: Name of the preprocessing workflow applied to the raw electrophysiology recording, such as eeglab_preprocess, custom_neuro_pipeline, or neurophysiology_pipeline_v1; record the implemented workflow used for this step.
Version string or release identifier for the preprocessing workflow used on the raw recordings; examples include 1.0.0, 2024.07, or a Git tag/commit label.
Execution environment used for the preprocessing step, such as Python, MATLAB, or a containerized runtime, recorded at the process level for reproducibility.

Lower cutoff frequency used for filtering the raw recordings during preprocessing, measured in hertz and applied at the start of the filtering stage; typical range is approximately 0.1-300 Hz depending on channel type.

Upper cutoff frequency used for filtering the raw recordings during preprocessing, measured in hertz and applied during signal conditioning; typical range depends on whether the channel is LFP-oriented or spike-oriented.
Notch filter center frequency used to suppress line noise during preprocessing, measured in hertz; common values are 50 or 60 Hz and may include harmonics.
Method used to synchronize electrophysiology channels or align recording segments during preprocessing, such as shared_clock, event_marker_alignment, or sample_offset_correction.
Whether artifact rejection or segment exclusion was applied during preprocessing to remove gross contamination or invalid samples before downstream analysis.
Method used to identify and remove artifacts during preprocessing, such as threshold_based, manual_curation, or automated_detector, if artifact rejection was enabled.
Operator or pipeline-assessed quality of the preprocessing result at the end of this process, indicating whether the cleaned recording is suitable for downstream spike and LFP analysis.

preprocessed_lfp_signal.reasoning: The preprocessed_lfp_signal node is a Signal, so I included only cleaned signal artefact metadata that distinguish it from the raw LFP file and support downstream reuse: artefact identity, storage, shape, filtering summary, and quality of the processed LFP stream. I excluded preprocessing protocol parameters because those belong to the upstream process node, and I excluded feature extraction or alignment outputs because those belong to downstream derivative nodes. Since many generic signal field names have already been used elsewhere in the DAG, I chose LFP-specific names that avoid collisions while remaining faithful to the signal-layer scope.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the cleaned LFP signal object; use a stable code such as lfp_clean_001 or a UUID. This identifies the processed signal artefact itself.
File system or object-store location of the preprocessed LFP artefact, such as a directory path, URI, or bucket/key reference used for retrieval.
Digital file format of the preprocessed LFP artefact, recorded as the storage encoding used for the processed signal; examples include nwb, hdf5, mat, or bin.
Number of LFP channels present in the cleaned signal object after preprocessing; typically corresponds to channels retained after artifact rejection or trimming.
Number of time samples in the cleaned LFP trace after preprocessing, counted across the stored signal object; this may differ from the raw length if segments were trimmed or removed.
Time unit used to represent sample timing or timestamps in the preprocessed LFP file; record the unit applied to the stored cleaned signal representation.
Technical quality status of the cleaned LFP signal at the signal level, indicating whether the preprocessed artefact is suitable for feature extraction and alignment.

Concise summary of the applied cleaning or filtering represented in the signal object, such as bandpass_range_1_100hz, notch_60hz_applied, or artifact_trimmed; this summarizes the state of the signal rather than the process parameters.
Numeric representation used to store the cleaned LFP samples in the processed artefact, such as int16, int32, or float32, if known from the exported file.
Physical units used for the preprocessed LFP values in the stored artefact; typical value is microvolts for cortical extracellular recordings.

preprocessed_spike_signal.reasoning: The preprocessed_spike_signal node is a Signal, so I included only processed signal artefact metadata needed to locate, inspect, and reuse the cleaned spike-oriented recording. I excluded filtering and synchronization parameters because those belong to the upstream preprocessing Process node, and I excluded spike detection/sorting outputs because those belong to downstream Process and Derivative nodes. To avoid repeating fields already used elsewhere in the DAG, I used preprocessed-specific names rather than generic signal identifiers. The selected fields describe the artefact state after cleaning, including storage, dimensions, file encoding, and signal-level quality.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the cleaned spike signal object; use a stable code such as spike_clean_001 or a UUID. This identifies the processed signal artefact itself.
File system or object-store location of the preprocessed spike artefact, such as a directory path, URI, or bucket/key reference used for retrieval.
Digital file format of the preprocessed spike artefact, recorded as the storage encoding used for the processed signal; examples include nwb, hdf5, mat, or bin.
Number of spike channels present in the cleaned signal object after preprocessing; typically corresponds to channels retained for spike detection or sorting.
Number of time samples in the cleaned spike trace after preprocessing, counted across the stored signal object; this may differ from the raw length if segments were trimmed or removed.
Time unit used to represent sample timing or timestamps in the preprocessed spike file; record the unit applied to the stored cleaned signal representation.
Technical quality status of the cleaned spike signal at the signal level, indicating whether the preprocessed artefact is suitable for spike detection or sorting.

Concise summary of the applied cleaning or filtering represented in the signal object, such as bandpass_range_300_5000hz, notch_60hz_applied, or artifact_trimmed; this summarizes the state of the signal rather than the process parameters.
Numeric representation used to store the cleaned spike samples in the processed artefact, such as int16, int32, or float32, if known from the exported file.
Physical units used for the preprocessed spike voltage values in the stored artefact; typical value is microvolts for extracellular spike recordings.

spike_sorting.reasoning: The spike_sorting node is a Process, so I included only computation-level fields that describe how spike waveforms were detected and clustered from the preprocessed spike signal. I excluded raw/preprocessed signal file properties and the resulting unit table or spike train properties because those belong to the input Signal nodes or the downstream Derivative node. To avoid collisions with earlier process metadata, I used spike-sorting-specific names rather than generic processing identifiers. The selected fields capture the algorithm, key thresholds, and an output-quality indicator for reproducibility and interpretation.

md_schema.descr: Name of the spike sorting workflow used to detect and cluster waveforms from the preprocessed spike signal, such as spikesort_v1, kilosort, or spikeinterface_pipeline.
Version string or release identifier for the spike sorting workflow, such as 1.0.0, 0.9.1, or a Git tag/commit label.
Execution environment or software stack used for spike sorting, such as Python, MATLAB, or a containerized runtime, recorded at the process level for reproducibility.
Primary algorithm used to detect and cluster spike waveforms from the preprocessed signal, such as kilosort2, mountainsort4, template_matching, or threshold_based_sorting.
Detection threshold used for spike event identification, expressed as a multiple of the estimated noise standard deviation; typical range is approximately 2-8 sigma.
Time window used to extract each candidate spike waveform around the detection point, measured in milliseconds; typical range is approximately 0.5-5 ms.
Minimum inter-spike interval constraint used during sorting or curation to separate candidate events, measured in milliseconds; typical range is approximately 0.5-5 ms.
Method used to curate or accept putative neuronal units after initial spike detection and clustering, such as manual_curation, automated_curation, or none.
Overall quality status of the sorting result at the end of the process, indicating whether the clustering output is suitable for downstream spike-train derivation.

sorted_spike_trains.reasoning: The sorted_spike_trains node is a Derivative, so I included only computed-result metadata describing the inferred spike-train output: identity, unit count, spike counts, time coverage, representation, and analysis-quality indicators. I excluded spike-sorting algorithm parameters because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded raw or preprocessed signal properties because those belong to Signal nodes. I also avoided fields already used elsewhere in the DAG by naming the output-specific identifiers and metrics in a derivative-specific way. The selected fields are sufficient for downstream users to understand the structure and reliability of the inferred neuronal firing patterns.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the derived spike-train dataset; use a stable code such as spikes_sorted_001 or a UUID. This identifies the computed output object itself.
Number of putative neuronal units represented in the sorted spike-train derivative; this is the count of distinct clustered units output by spike sorting.
Total number of spike events aggregated across all sorted units in the derivative, counted over the stored analysis interval; typical range depends on session length and firing rates.
Start time of the interval represented by the sorted spike-train derivative, measured in seconds relative to the recording/session reference frame.
End time of the interval represented by the sorted spike-train derivative, measured in seconds relative to the recording/session reference frame.
Data representation used for the sorted spike-train output, such as event_times, binned_counts, or unit_by_time_matrix, as stored in the derivative.
Temporal bin width used if the sorted spike-train derivative is represented as binned counts or matrices, measured in milliseconds; use null-equivalent omission if event_times are stored instead.
Derived quality assessment of the unit assignments in the sorted spike trains, indicating confidence in the clustering output for downstream analysis.
Brief reference to the sorting method used to generate the derivative, such as the sorter name or algorithm label recorded for traceability at the output level.

lfp_feature_extraction.reasoning: The lfp_feature_extraction node is a Process, so I included only transformation-level metadata describing how cleaned LFP signals were converted into features, including the feature method, parameterization, analysis windowing, and an output-quality indicator. I excluded signal file properties and feature outputs themselves because those belong to the input Signal and downstream Derivative nodes. To avoid collisions with earlier process fields, I used LFP-specific names rather than generic processing identifiers. The selected fields are enough for a downstream user to reproduce the extraction workflow without describing the resulting feature table.

md_schema.descr: Name of the LFP feature extraction workflow used to transform cleaned LFP time series into analyzable features, such as mne_feature_pipeline, scipy_bandpower_pipeline, or custom_lfp_extractor.
Version string or release identifier for the LFP feature extraction workflow, such as 1.0.0, 2024.08, or a Git tag/commit label.
Execution environment or software stack used for LFP feature extraction, such as Python, MATLAB, or a containerized runtime, recorded at the process level for reproducibility.
Named set of LFP features computed in this step, such as bandpower, event_related_potential, spectral_summary, or mixed_feature_set.
Lower bound of the frequency band used for band-limited LFP feature computation, measured in hertz; typical range is approximately 0.5-100 Hz depending on the feature.
Upper bound of the frequency band used for band-limited LFP feature computation, measured in hertz; typical range is approximately 1-200 Hz depending on the feature.
Length of the analysis window used to compute LFP features, measured in milliseconds; typical range is approximately 10-5000 ms depending on the feature type.
Fractional overlap between adjacent analysis windows used during feature extraction, expressed as a value between 0 and 1; use 0 when no overlap is applied.
Method used to normalize LFP features during extraction, such as z_score, baseline_subtraction, log_transform, or none.
Overall quality status of the feature extraction result at the end of the process, indicating whether the transformed output is suitable for downstream analysis.

lfp_features.reasoning: The lfp_features node is a Derivative, so I kept only computed-result metadata for the derived LFP object: identity, feature content, dimensionality, time coverage, and quality. I removed any process-parameter or signal-level details because they belong upstream or downstream. Because analysis_time_start_seconds and analysis_time_end_seconds were already used elsewhere in the DAG, I replaced them with LFP-specific, non-colliding names that still express the derivative time span. The remaining fields are sufficient for interpreting the derived feature set without duplicating earlier metadata.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the derived LFP feature dataset; use a stable code such as lfp_feat_001 or a UUID. This identifies the computed output object itself.
Named collection of derived LFP features contained in this object, such as bandpower, event_related_potential, spectral_summary, or mixed_feature_set.
Total number of distinct LFP features represented in the derivative, counted across all channels, bands, and windows included in the output.
Number of LFP channels contributing to the derived feature object; this usually reflects the channels retained after preprocessing and feature extraction.

Start time of the interval represented by the derived LFP features, measured in seconds relative to the recording/session reference frame; use this instead of a generic analysis time field to avoid collision with other DAG steps.

End time of the interval represented by the derived LFP features, measured in seconds relative to the recording/session reference frame; use this instead of a generic analysis time field to avoid collision with other DAG steps.
Shape of the derived feature matrix, recorded as rows_by_columns or an equivalent structured description such as channels_by_features or trials_by_features; this describes the output dimensionality.
Physical or normalized units of the derived LFP feature values, such as microvolts, microvolts_squared, power_ratio, or arbitrary_units, depending on the computed measure.
Derived quality assessment of the LFP feature output, indicating whether the computed features are suitable for downstream association with task and behavior.
Optional summary statistic used to characterize the derived LFP features at output time, such as mean_power, peak_amplitude, or event_locked_response_strength.

stimulus_parameters.reasoning: The stimulus_parameters node is a Derivative, so I included only computed or curated trial/stimulus descriptors that summarize the digital parameters used during the behavioral session. I excluded capture hardware settings, raw signal properties, and process parameters because those belong to Capture, Signal, or Process nodes. I also avoided the already-colliding analysis_time_start_seconds and analysis_time_end_seconds fields, since they were previously generated elsewhere in the DAG. The chosen fields focus on stimulus identity, timing, intensity, condition structure, and trial-level quality so downstream users can align stimuli with neural and behavioral data.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the stimulus parameter table or object; use a stable code such as stim_params_001 or a UUID. This identifies the curated stimulus-parameter derivative itself.
Name of the behavioral stimulus protocol or task variant used during the recording session, such as decision_task, go_nogo_task, or visual_discrimination.
Type of stimulus delivered or represented in the session, such as auditory, visual, tactile, multimodal, or sham_control.
Number of trials represented in the stimulus-parameter derivative, counted across the session or selected analysis interval.
Number of distinct stimulus conditions encoded in the table, such as combinations of cue type, reward state, or difficulty level.
Duration of each stimulus presentation or trial epoch, measured in milliseconds; typical range depends on task design and may span tens to thousands of milliseconds.
Average or nominal interval between trials, measured in milliseconds, as represented in the stimulus-parameter derivative.
Stimulus intensity or contrast level used in the session, recorded as the task-specific numeric scale or normalized level applied during delivery.
Primary categorical label associated with each trial condition in the stimulus table, such as hit, miss, correct_rejection, false_alarm, or neutral.
Quality status of the stimulus-parameter derivative, indicating whether the encoded trial and condition information is suitable for downstream alignment and analysis.

behavioral_annotations.reasoning: The behavioral_annotations node is a Derivative, so I included only computed/curated behavioral-event metadata that describes the annotated session output itself. I excluded subject identity, stimulus parameters, and capture or preprocessing details because those belong to Entity, Derivative, Capture, or Process nodes elsewhere in the DAG. I also avoided time-range fields that were already generated previously in the DAG, and focused instead on annotation content, label structure, timing granularity, and quality of the annotation output. These fields are sufficient for a downstream user to interpret and align behavioral events with neural data.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the behavioral annotation dataset or object; use a stable code such as beh_ann_001 or a UUID. This identifies the derived annotation output itself.
Name of the behavioral annotation scheme or coding rubric applied to the session, such as task_state_labels, event_annotation_v1, or behavior_coding_schema.
Total number of annotated behavioral events represented in the derivative, counted across the aligned recording session or analysis interval.
Number of distinct task-state labels used in the annotation set, such as cue, choice, reward, or inter_trial_interval.
List or summary category of behavioral event types included in the annotations, such as lick, lever_press, nose_poke, movement_onset, or reward_delivery.
Set of task-state labels assigned to behavioral intervals in the annotation output, representing the coded behavioral context of the session.
Temporal resolution used to place behavioral annotations on the session timeline, measured in milliseconds; typical range is 1-100 ms depending on the coding method.
Origin of the behavioral annotations, such as manual_curation, automated_tracking, video_synchronization, or mixed_source.
Overall quality status of the behavioral annotation derivative, indicating whether the labels are suitable for downstream alignment and analysis.

task_alignment.reasoning: The task_alignment node is a Process, so I included only alignment-method metadata describing how stimulus, behavioral, spike, and LFP inputs were synchronized into a common trial/time reference. I excluded upstream input content and downstream aligned-table outputs because those belong to the incoming Derivative nodes and outgoing Derivative node, respectively. To avoid collisions with previously generated fields, I used alignment-specific names rather than generic process labels. The selected fields capture the alignment reference, matching strategy, correction behavior, and process-level quality needed for reproducibility.

md_schema.descr: Name of the alignment workflow used to synchronize stimulus, behavior, spike, and LFP inputs, such as trial_alignment_pipeline, event_sync_pipeline, or custom_alignment_v1.
Version string or release identifier for the alignment workflow, such as 1.0.0, 2024.08, or a Git tag/commit label.
Execution environment or software stack used for alignment, such as Python, MATLAB, or a containerized runtime, recorded at the process level for reproducibility.
Reference frame used to place all inputs onto a common timeline, such as trial_start, stimulus_onset, behavior_onset, or session_clock.
Primary method used to align the data streams, such as event_marker_matching, clock_drift_correction, cross_correlation, or manual_mapping.
Net time shift applied during alignment to correct offsets between data streams, measured in milliseconds; typical range may be negative or positive depending on lag direction.
Whether long-duration drift correction was applied during alignment to maintain synchrony across the recording session.
Fraction or percentage of trials successfully matched across stimulus, behavior, spike, and LFP inputs during alignment; values are expected to be between 0 and 1 if stored as a fraction.
Overall quality status of the alignment result at the end of the process, indicating whether the synchronized frame is suitable for downstream joint analysis.

aligned_session_table.reasoning: The aligned_session_table node is a Derivative, so I included only computed-output metadata describing the synchronized table itself: identity, composition, size, key structural dimensions, and quality of the aligned dataset. I excluded alignment procedure details because those belong to the upstream task_alignment Process node, and I excluded source raw/preprocessed signal properties because those belong to Signal and earlier Derivative nodes. I also avoided time-range fields that were already generated elsewhere in the DAG, and used table-specific names that do not collide with prior metadata fields. These fields are sufficient for a downstream user to understand the aligned analysis frame and the structure of the table they will analyze.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the synchronized session table; use a stable code such as aligned_tbl_001 or a UUID. This identifies the derived table object itself.
Total number of rows in the aligned session table, typically corresponding to trials, time bins, or aligned event records depending on the chosen analysis frame.
Total number of columns in the aligned session table, including neural features, stimulus parameters, behavioral annotations, and identifier columns.
Primary unit of alignment represented by the table, such as trial, event, or time_bin; this describes the common analysis frame used in the synchronized derivative.
Modalities combined into the aligned table, such as neural_features, stimulus_parameters, and behavioral_annotations; record the major source classes present in the output.
Fraction of table entries that are missing or null after alignment and integration, expressed as a value between 0 and 1; lower values indicate a more complete table.
Derived score summarizing the internal consistency of the aligned session table after integration, such as match completeness or synchronization confidence, recorded on the table output.
Storage representation of the aligned session table, such as csv, parquet, hdf5, or nwb_table, as exported for downstream analysis.
Overall quality status of the aligned session table, indicating whether the synchronized derivative is suitable for downstream joint analysis.

decision_analysis.reasoning: The decision_analysis node is a Process, so I included only analysis-level metadata describing how aligned derivatives were interrogated to identify decision-making correlates. I excluded source data properties and final result fields because those belong to upstream Derivative nodes and the downstream decision_making_results node, respectively. To avoid collisions with earlier process metadata, I used analysis-specific names rather than generic pipeline labels. The selected fields capture the statistical/modeling approach, target outcomes, covariates, and process-level quality needed to reproduce the analysis without describing the outputs themselves.

md_schema.descr: Name of the decision-correlation analysis workflow used on the aligned session table, such as decision_glm_pipeline, neural_behavior_correlation_pipeline, or custom_stats_pipeline.
Version string or release identifier for the analysis workflow, such as 1.0.0, 2024.08, or a Git tag/commit label.
Execution environment or software stack used for decision analysis, such as Python, R, MATLAB, or a containerized runtime, recorded at the process level for reproducibility.
Primary analytical method used to identify decision-making correlates, such as logistic_regression, generalized_linear_model, mixed_effects_model, correlation_analysis, or decoder_based_analysis.
Decision-related outcome variable tested in the analysis, such as choice, correctness, reaction_time, or reward_selection.
Number of predictor variables or covariates included in the analysis model, counted at the process setup stage.
Whether cross-validation or holdout evaluation was used during the analysis to assess generalization of the decision-correlation model.
Correction method used to control false positives across multiple tests, such as bonferroni, fdr_bh, permutation_based, or none.
Overall quality status of the decision-analysis process, indicating whether the analysis is suitable for interpretation and for generating downstream results.

decision_making_results.reasoning: The decision_making_results node is a Derivative, so I included only computed-output metadata describing the analysis results object itself: identity, model fit summaries, effect sizes, statistical significance, predictive performance, and result-level quality. I excluded the analysis protocol and modeling parameters because those belong to the upstream decision_analysis Process node, and I excluded raw/aligned input properties because those belong to earlier Signal and Derivative nodes. I also avoided field names that would collide with previously generated DAG steps by using result-specific names. These fields are sufficient for a downstream user to interpret the decision-making conclusions and assess confidence in the integrated outputs.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the decision analysis result object; use a stable code such as decision_res_001 or a UUID. This identifies the computed output itself.
Name of the statistical or predictive model whose outputs are stored in this results object, such as logistic_regression, glm, mixed_effects_model, or decoder_based_analysis.
Total number of result entries contained in the output, such as coefficients, contrasts, units, or model summaries, depending on the analysis design.
Number of result entries passing the chosen significance or threshold criterion in the final analysis output.
Primary effect-size metric reported by the analysis, such as odds_ratio, beta_coefficient, correlation_coefficient, or auc, depending on the model type.
Numerical value of the primary effect-size metric for the main decision-related association, reported on the scale implied by effect_size_metric.
Significance threshold used to classify decision-related results as notable in the output, typically a value such as 0.05 or 0.01.
Performance score summarizing predictive or explanatory quality of the final decision-analysis model, such as accuracy, auc, r_squared, or cross-validated score.
Overall quality status of the decision-making results object, indicating whether the output is suitable for interpretation and reporting.
